title: What is a marker interface, what are examples (`Serializable`, `Cloneable`, `Remote`), and can you create a custom one?
shortTitle: What is a marker interface and what are the examples?

s1_definition.profdef: A marker interface is an interface with no methods and no fields that is used purely to tag a class with a piece of metadata. The presence of the interface signals to the Java virtual machine, a library, or a framework that the class is allowed to participate in some behavior, and code checks for it with the `instanceof` operator. Classic examples are `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, and `Remote`. Since Java 5, annotations are generally the preferred way to attach metadata, but marker interfaces still have the advantage of being a type, so they can be enforced at compile time and used in method signatures.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a marker interface like a special colored sticker the National Bank of India compliance team puts on certain account folders. The sticker has no instructions written on it; it simply means "this folder is approved to be archived to the central vault." When the archiving clerk picks up a folder, he only checks whether the sticker is present. If it is there, he archives it; if not, he refuses. The sticker carries no methods, only permission. That is exactly what `Serializable` does: it carries no methods, it just marks a class as allowed to be turned into bytes.
s1_definition.oneliner: A marker interface is an empty interface used as a type-level tag so that the JVM or a framework can check with instanceof whether a class is permitted to take part in some behavior.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A marker interface is an interface with no methods and no fields that is used purely to tag a class with a piece of metadata. The presence of the interface signals to the Java virtual machine, a library, or a framework that the class is allowed to participate in some behavior, and code checks for it with the `instanceof` operator. Classic examples are `Serializable`, `Cloneable`, and `Remote`. Since Java 5, annotations are generally the preferred way to attach metadata, but marker interfaces still have the advantage of being a type, so they can be enforced at compile time and used in method signatures.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a marker interface like a special colored sticker the National Bank of India compliance team puts on certain account folders. The sticker has no instructions written on it; it simply means "this folder is approved to be archived to the central vault." When the archiving clerk picks up a folder, he only checks whether the sticker is present. If it is there, he archives it; if not, he refuses. The sticker carries no methods, only permission. That is exactly what `Serializable` does: it carries no methods, it just marks a class as allowed to be turned into bytes.

**One line to remember:** A marker interface is an empty interface used as a type-level tag so that the JVM or a framework can check with instanceof whether a class is permitted to take part in some behavior.

sections.s2_technical:
A marker interface declares no methods, so implementing it forces no code on you. Its only job is to attach a type to a class. The runtime or a library then tests that type. The classic example is `java.io.Serializable`. When you call `ObjectOutputStream.writeObject`, the serialization machinery checks `if (obj instanceof Serializable)`; if the object is not marked, it throws `NotSerializableException`. The interface has no methods, yet it changes what the JVM allows.

`Cloneable` works similarly. The `Object.clone` method is protected and native, and it checks whether the object implements `Cloneable`; if not, it throws `CloneNotSupportedException`. Here is a small banking usage: `class Account implements Cloneable, Serializable { ... }` allows an Account both to be field-copied by clone and to be written to a byte stream. `java.rmi.Remote` is the third classic example; it marks objects whose methods can be invoked from another JVM over remote method invocation.

You can absolutely create your own marker interface. For example, in a banking system I might define `interface Auditable {}` and tag only those entities whose changes must be written to the audit log. An audit component then does `if (entity instanceof Auditable) auditLog.record(entity);`. The code example is simply `public interface Auditable { }` with nothing inside, and then `class Account implements Auditable { }`. The value is that only correctly tagged entities get audited, and the check is a cheap instanceof.

The senior-level comparison is marker interface versus annotation. Since Java 5 you could instead write `@Auditable` as an annotation and check for it with reflection. Annotations are often preferred because they can carry parameters, can be applied to methods and fields as well as types, and do not pollute the type hierarchy. However, a marker interface has one real advantage: it is a type, so it participates in the compiler's type system. You can write a method that accepts only `Auditable` objects, and the compiler will reject anything untagged at compile time, whereas an annotation check only fails at runtime. A subtle point is that a marker interface is inherited by subclasses, so once a base class implements `Serializable`, every subclass is serializable whether it wants to be or not, which is occasionally undesirable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores many kinds of records in memory, but only some of them, like accounts and transfers, must be archived to the central vault as bytes. Temporary objects like a live user session must never be archived. This is exactly what the `Serializable` marker interface controls, because only classes that carry that tag are allowed to be written to a byte stream, and everything else is rejected.

Problem 2 — The compliance team requires that every change to certain sensitive entities is written to the audit trail, but not every object in the system needs auditing. This is exactly what a custom marker interface solves, because we tag only the sensitive entities with our own `Auditable` marker, and the audit component checks for that tag with instanceof before recording anything.

In the mini-project we define a custom `Auditable` marker interface, make `Account` implement both `Serializable` and our `Auditable`, and leave a transient `LoginSession` unmarked. An `ArchiveService` tries to serialize objects and an `AuditService` records only auditable ones, logging which objects pass each gate and which are rejected.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one `Account` for Rajesh marked with both `Serializable` and `Auditable`, and one `LoginSession` that carries neither marker.

Step 1: Main passes the Account to `ArchiveService.tryArchive`. The service does an instanceof Serializable check. The Account is marked, so the check passes and the data flows to the ObjectOutputStream, which turns it into bytes.

Step 2: Main passes the LoginSession to the same method. The instanceof Serializable check fails because the class carries no such tag, so the data never reaches the stream and the service logs a rejection. The LoginSession stays exactly as it was in memory.

Step 3: Main passes the Account to `AuditService.recordIfAuditable`. The service checks instanceof Auditable, our custom marker. The Account carries it, so an audit entry is recorded.

Step 4: Main passes the LoginSession to the audit service. The instanceof Auditable check fails, so no audit entry is written and the object is skipped.

```text
[INFO] Archived Account as 93 bytes
[SEVERE] REJECTED archive: LoginSession is not Serializable
[INFO] AUDIT recorded change for Account
```

    Pre:  entity != null
    Post: audit written IFF entity instanceof Auditable

sections.s6_takeaway:
A marker interface is an interface that declares no methods and no fields, and its only purpose is to tag a class with a piece of metadata. Because it has no methods, implementing it costs you no code; the mere presence of the interface on a class is the signal. The Java virtual machine, a library, or a framework then checks for that tag, almost always with the instanceof operator, and uses the result to decide whether the class is permitted to take part in some behavior. The three classic examples are Serializable, which permits an object to be written to a byte stream, Cloneable, which permits the protected Object clone method to field-copy an object, and Remote, which marks objects callable across virtual machines through remote method invocation.

The way I always explain the mechanism is with Serializable. When you call writeObject on an ObjectOutputStream, the serialization machinery itself checks whether the object is an instance of Serializable, and if it is not, it throws a NotSerializableException. The interface has no methods, yet its presence changes what the runtime allows. Cloneable behaves the same way: Object clone checks for it and throws CloneNotSupportedException when it is missing.

Yes, you can absolutely create your own marker interface, and I have. In a banking system I defined an empty Auditable interface and tagged only the sensitive entities, like accounts and transfers, whose changes must be recorded. The audit component then does a simple instanceof Auditable check before writing to the audit trail, so unmarked objects like a transient login session are skipped automatically. This keeps the audit logic from having to know every class by name.

The senior point I like to close on is the comparison with annotations. Since Java 5 you can attach metadata with an annotation like an at-sign Auditable and read it with reflection, and annotations are often preferred because they can carry parameters, apply to methods and fields, and do not add to the type hierarchy. The one real advantage a marker interface keeps is that it is a genuine type, so I can write a method that accepts only Auditable objects and the compiler enforces it at compile time, whereas an annotation check only fails at runtime. The trade-off I always mention is that a marker interface is inherited by every subclass, so once a base class is Serializable, every subclass becomes serializable whether that was intended or not.

---

keyPoints: Marker interface: zero methods — signals a capability to the JVM or framework
Serializable: marks object as safe for byte-stream serialization
Cloneable: marks object as safe for Object.clone()
Remote: marks object as available for RMI
Modern alternative: annotations (@Entity, @Component) replace most marker interfaces
